items.title: What the delimitation fight means and why this time is different
items.summary: Seven months after its delimitation plan was voted down, the government is trying again. Parliament reconvenes on Monday for a four-day sitting on a question India has put off for half a century: how many Lok Sabha seats each state should get. Seat shares have been frozen at 1971 population figures since 1976. That freeze lapses once the next census is published, and the government wants the terms settled before then. The April bill, the Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill, would have raised the Lok Sabha’s maximum strength from 543 to 850 and tied the expansion to the 33 percent reservation for women. It fell short of a two-thirds majority, 298 votes to 230 against the 352 it needed, and the government withdrew the accompanying Delimitation Bill, 2026. This time, the Union Cabinet has approved a different bill. The Constitution Bill (132nd Amendment) would write a uniform 50 percent increase in every state’s seats into the Constitution, raise the cap on the Lok Sabha to 850, and extend the freeze on each state’s share of seats to 2051. items.title: Karnataka High Court directs courts to accept digital copies of HC orders without insisting on physical certification
items.summary: The Karnataka High Court has directed all courts and tribunals under its administrative and supervisory control to accept digitally signed copies of its daily and final orders and not insist on physical certified copies. The directive was issued through a circular dated November 25 and came into effect on November 26. The circular states that orders and judgments downloaded in PDF format from the High Court's official website, bearing a digital signature and QR code, shall be accepted by subordinate courts and tribunals. It further clarifies that the authenticity of such orders can be verified through the digital signature, QR code or any other verification mechanism provided on the High Court's official website. “The Courts shall extend full cooperation in giving effect to the digitization initiative and shall not insist upon physical certification where the order is capable of electronic verification,” the circular states. The circular was issued by order of the Chief Justice and signed by Registrar General M Chandrashekar Reddy. The communication has been addressed to all Principal District and Sessions Judges and Unit Heads across Karnataka. [Read Circular]

items.title: Karnataka High Court introduces RFID-based case file tracking system
items.summary: The Karnataka High Court has introduced an RFID-based File Tracking Module across all its registry branches to monitor the movement of case files, identify delays and improve the efficiency of file processing. In a circular dated November 24, Registrar General M Chandrashekar Reddy directed all concerned officials to strictly implement the system with effect from November 26. The initiative is part of the High Court's ongoing process of scanning and digitizing case files. RFID tags have been affixed to newly instituted cases at filing counters since June 2026. Tags are also being affixed to cases instituted before June 2026 as and when they are posted. The web-based module, developed by the High Court's engineers, links case file details with RFID tags and records the movement of files across different branches. It also enables the monitoring of the time taken by individual branches and staff members to process files and helps track their location from filing until disposal. Under the new instructions, every staff member must log into the module using their individual login credentials and scan the RFID tag of each file immediately upon receipt and before dispatch.
